# Paper 1 · the whole draft

*The title, the abstract and the authors' credit are left to the end. This is the current state of everything else,
regenerated from the code and its data on every change; the making is public at four.mino.mobi/papers.*

## Abstract

*To be written last.*

## 1 · Introduction

Why does space have three dimensions? Ehrenfest (1917, 1920) turned the question into physics. He asked what in the
laws of physics would change with the number of dimensions, and found, among other things, that under the
inverse-power force Gauss's law gives in $D$ dimensions, no planetary orbit is stable for $D > 3$. Tangherlini (1963)
carried the argument into general relativity and into quantum mechanics: the hydrogen atom with Gauss's potential has
no stable states above three dimensions. The usual conclusion is that a world with more than three large dimensions
has no atoms. Callender (2005) points out what that conclusion leans on, that the laws carry over to other dimensions
unchanged.

They needn't. The literature on the hydrogen atom in $D$ dimensions (Nieto 1979; Al-Jaber 1998) and on dimensional
scaling (Herschbach, Avery and Goscinski 1992; Loeser and Herschbach 1986) keeps the potential at $1/r$ in every $D$,
mostly as a convention that keeps the problem solvable. With it, hydrogen has a Bohr radius in any dimension. Négadi
and Kibler (1996) used the $D$-dimensional hydrogen atom to extend Madelung's filling rule (Madelung 1936) to other
dimensions, and predicted the rows of a four-dimensional periodic table. Pyykkö and Zhao (1991) solved the atoms of a
two-dimensional world self-consistently. To our knowledge no one has solved the atoms of a four-dimensional one, nor
asked what the choice of $1/r$ itself does to them.

This paper does both. Part I treats the law as a choice. It shows why one has to be made (section 2), why $1/r$ exactly
(section 3), and what it costs in four dimensions (section 4). Part II solves every neutral atom to $Z = 140$ under it
(sections 5–8). It checks the same solver against our own table (section 6). It finds that four-dimensional space
breaks Hund's first rule, which the solver had assumed, and corrects for it (section 7), and it gives the table
(section 8). Part III asks which of the table's features the law decides. It solves the table a second time with the
shell theorem forced back on (section 9), and follows the law into partial screening (section 10) and into the pull of
neutral atoms (section 11). Section 12 states the limitations; section 13 concludes.

Every number in the text is recomputed from the code and its baked data each time anything changes, and is checked
against a ledger of 31 claims. The code, the data and the paper's own making are public at
four.mino.mobi/papers.

# Part I · The law


## 2 · Why a law has to be chosen

Ask what the atoms are in a world with four dimensions of space and there is no answer yet, because the question
leaves out the law between charges. In our world that law isn't a free choice. Gauss's law, which is what a local,
linear field theory of charge gives, says the field of a point charge spreads over the sphere around it; the sphere's
area grows as $r^{D-1}$, so the potential falls as $r^{-(D-2)}$. In three dimensions that is $1/r$. In four it is
$1/r^2$, and with $1/r^2$ there are no atoms.

**2.1 Gauss's law leaves no atom.** One electron in $V = -\alpha/r^2$ has a Hamiltonian with no length in it: stretch
every distance by a factor and the kinetic and potential energies scale alike. In four dimensions Hardy's inequality
puts a floor under the kinetic energy,

$$\int |\nabla\psi|^2 \;\ge\; \Big(\frac{D-2}{2}\Big)^2 \int \frac{|\psi|^2}{r^2} \;=\; \int \frac{|\psi|^2}{r^2} \quad (D = 4),$$

so with the kinetic energy $\tfrac12|\nabla\psi|^2$ the pull wins only for $\alpha > \tfrac12$. Below that nothing binds;
above it the electron falls to the centre (Case 1950). We solved it rather than argue it (section 5, `laws.js`): for
$\alpha = 0.45$ there is no bound level on any grid, and for $\alpha = 0.7$ the lowest level is −5.87 × 10³,
−5.87 × 10⁵ and −5.87 × 10⁷ hartree on grids whose inner end is $10^{-3}$, $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-5}$ bohr: it grows as
$1/r_0^2$ ($\varepsilon r_0^2$ = −0.00587, −0.00587), set by where the calculation stops rather than by the
electron (figure 2a). Either way there is no Bohr radius, no size an atom could settle at. Ehrenfest made the
classical version of this argument in 1917: under Gauss's law in four dimensions no planetary orbit is stable either.

**2.2 The ways out, and what each costs.** Something has to give. The squeeze that resists the pull costs
$\hbar^2/2mr^2$ because the electron's energy grows as $p^2$; the pull costs $1/r^2$ because of Gauss. Change either and
a length comes back. One way is to change the electron: an energy growing as $p^3$ or $p^4$ outgrows a $1/r^2$ pull
close in, so atoms bind at every strength. It keeps Gauss's law, and with it the shell theorem and the Faraday cage, but
it gives up Galilean relativity for all matter: a moving laboratory and a still one see the same physics only if
energy is quadratic in momentum. Another is a small fourth dimension, the way extra dimensions could hide in ours; but
atoms larger than it are three-dimensional atoms and smaller ones fall again, so it doesn't give four-dimensional
chemistry. The third is to change the law: keep the electron, keep four large dimensions, and make the potential
between charges fall as $1/r$. This universe takes the third, and the rest of part I says why $1/r$ and what it costs.
The choice between the first and the third is a judgement, stated as one: the electron route keeps our Faraday cages,
the law route keeps our mechanics.

## 3 · Why 1/r, exactly

**3.1 Only 1/r keeps a shell together.** Among power laws $V = -1/r^p$, those with $0 < p < 2$ bind with a length of
their own. Only $p = 1$ has the hidden symmetry of the hydrogen problem, SO($D+1$) in $D$ dimensions (Fock 1935; Bander
and Itzykson 1966), which makes a level depend on $n$ alone: in four dimensions $-Z^2/2(n + \tfrac12)^2$, with every $l$
below $n$ at the same energy. That degeneracy is what makes a shell, and four-dimensional shells hold
$\sum_{l<n} 2(l+1)^2$ electrons: 2, 10, 28, 60. We measured how fast it breaks (figure 2b): the 2p level sits
−6.2 % from 2s at $p = 0.8$, 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ % at $p = 1$ and +15.4 % at $p = 1.2$ (as a fraction of the
shell's binding; 3d against 3s goes the same way). Below 1 the more-turning electron is the more bound, above it the
less, and either way the shell comes apart. The rows of the periodic table in section 8 rest on this.

**3.2 The convention it agrees with.** The literature on hydrogen in $D$ dimensions (Nieto 1979; Al-Jaber 1998) and on
dimensional scaling (Herschbach, Avery and Goscinski 1992) takes $1/r$ in every $D$, mostly as a convention that keeps
the problem solvable. Négadi and Kibler's generalized Madelung rule (1996), which predicts the four-dimensional rows,
builds on the same $D$-dimensional hydrogen atom. Section 3.1 is why that convention is more than one: it is the only power law under which the question
"what are the shells?" has the answer the rule needs.

## 4 · What 1/r costs in four dimensions

**4.1 It isn't harmonic.** In three dimensions $\nabla^2(1/r) = 0$ away from the charge, and that one fact is Gauss's
law. In $D$ dimensions $\nabla^2 r^q = q(q + D - 2)\,r^{q-2}$, so in four

$$\nabla^2 \frac{1}{r} = -\frac{1}{r^3} \qquad (r \ne 0),$$

which we check numerically (−1.00000 at $r = 1$, −0.12500 at $r = 2$). The flux of the field through a sphere
round a charge grows with the sphere's radius, linearly in four dimensions, as if empty space were charged with a
density $\propto 1/r^3$. There is no Gauss's law for it.

**4.2 No shell theorem, no Faraday cage.** A thin spherical shell of charge, felt at radius $r$, gives $k(t)/\max(r, s)$
with $t = \min/\max$ and $k$ the $1/r$ kernel averaged over the 3-sphere (section 5, appendix A). In three dimensions
$k = 1$: the shell theorem. In four, $k$ falls from 1 at the centre to $k(1) = 8/3\pi$ = 0.848826 at the shell
(figure A1). So a cloud of charge never acts as if it sat at its centre; a hollow conductor's centre sits at
$3\pi/8$ = 1.178097 of its wall's potential, and a charge inside is pushed toward the wall; and a neutral atom is
felt from outside, as $-\sum\langle r^2\rangle/8s^3$ at distance $s$ (section 11). Everything distinctive in part III
comes from here.

**4.3 A field theory for it.** In Maxwell's theory a charge's potential is the Fourier transform of $1/k^2$, which is
$1/r^2$ in four dimensions; $1/r$ needs $1/k^3$. The book's force chapter goes through five ways to get it:

1. *A local, relativistic field:* impossible. $1/k^3$ isn't a whole number of derivatives.
2. *Relativistic but non-local,* $\Box^{3/2}$: the field's scaling dimension is 1, below the unitarity
   bound of 1.5, so the theory has states of negative probability.
3. *A vacuum whose permittivity grows with wavenumber,* $\varepsilon(k) = \varepsilon_0 \ell k$: statics give $1/r$, but
   light disperses like deep-water waves, $\omega = c\sqrt{k/\ell}$, and there is no speed of light.
4. *A nonlinear vacuum,* $\nabla\cdot(|E|^{m-2}E) = \rho$ with $m$ = 2.5: $1/r$, but fields no longer add.
5. *A small fourth dimension:* $1/r$ far away, but then atoms are three-dimensional (section 2.2).

This universe takes a sixth, which finishes route 3: the **lens vacuum**, $\varepsilon(k) = \varepsilon_0 \ell k$ and
$\mu(k) = \mu_0/\ell k$. Then $D/\varepsilon_0$ and $\mu_0 H$ obey Maxwell's equations in empty four-dimensional space
exactly, so light is ordinary four-dimensional light at speed $c$ at every wavelength, and the energy is never negative.
What pushes a charge is that light seen through a lens, $E = (D/\varepsilon_0)/\ell k$, which blurs it across space with
a $1/r^3$ kernel; its statics are $1/\ell k^3$, the pinned $1/r$. The price is relativity, for the force between
charges only: the blur acts across all of space at once, so there is an absolute "now", and a charge feels another's
change instantly, a little, everywhere. Atoms are static, so nothing in this paper depends on $\ell$ or on the absolute
now; the field theory is the subject of a later paper.

**4.4 What is declared with it.** Electrons are spin-½ fermions, two to an orbital. That is stated, not derived: in our
world it follows from relativity and spin together, and this universe has given up relativity for the force. Nuclei
are point charges $+Z$, stable for every $Z$ to 140 (declared: nuclear physics in four dimensions is another paper). The
fine-structure constant is small, so atoms are solved without relativity (section 12). No other long-range field acts
on charges.

**4.5 Is matter stable?** In ours it is a theorem that $N$ atoms have an energy proportional to $N$ (Dyson and Lenard
1967; Lieb and Thirring 1975), and the proofs lean on the shell theorem, which fails here. So we give evidence, not a
proof. Atoms don't collapse: Thomas–Fermi scaling gives total energies growing as $Z^{3-2/D}$, $Z^{7/3}$ in ours and
$Z^{5/2}$ in four dimensions (Kventsel and Katriel 1981), and the solved table follows it, with a fitted exponent of
2.527 over $Z$ = 10–140 (ours: 2.387 over 10–36; both a little above the asymptotic value, as finite-$Z$
corrections make them). Many atoms don't run away either: every force between neutral atoms here (the permanent
$-3S_AS_B/64R^5$ of section 11, dispersion's $R^{-6}$) falls faster than $R^{-4}$, so summed over four-dimensional space
each atom's share is finite. This is argued, not proved, and the paper says so.

# Part II · The table

## 5 · Methods

### The law inside an atom

An atom here is a point nucleus of charge Z and Z electrons, non-relativistic, with every pair of charges interacting
through the pinned potential q₁q₂/r in four spatial dimensions. The same law acts between an electron and the nucleus
and between two electrons; nothing in the method borrows Gauss's law. Atomic units throughout (hartree, bohr).

Each electron moves in the field of the nucleus and of the other electrons' clouds, averaged over directions, so the
problem is radial. In D dimensions a wavefunction $R(r)\,Y_l$, written as $u = r^{(D-1)/2} R$, obeys

$$-\tfrac12\,u'' + \Big[\frac{L(L+1)}{2r^2} + V(r)\Big]\,u = \varepsilon\,u, \qquad L = l + \frac{D-3}{2},$$

so four dimensions differ from ours by the half-integer shift of L (L = l + ½) and by the degeneracies: a subshell of
angular momentum l holds 2(2l + 1) electrons in ours and 2(l + 1)² in four dimensions. With V = −Z/r the levels are
−Z²/2(n + (D − 3)/2)², so 4D hydrogen's ground state is −2/9 hartree; the solver gives −0.22222 (section 7).

**The clouds' potential.** A spherical shell of charge at radius s, felt at radius r, gives in ours 1/max(r, s) (the
shell theorem). In four dimensions under 1/r it gives k(t)/max(r, s), t = min/max, with k the 1/r kernel averaged over
a 3-sphere,

$$k(t) = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \frac{\sin^2\theta\,d\theta}{\sqrt{1 + t^2 - 2t\cos\theta}},$$

which falls from k(0) = 1 to k(1) = 8/3π = 0.848826 (appendix A; Simpson's rule on 400 intervals, then a
table of 2001 points with linear interpolation). Every electron–electron term in the self-consistent
field, its energy and the ionized atom's goes through this kernel. That is where the missing shell theorem enters the
atom: an inner cloud screens the nucleus from an outer electron only partly.

**Exchange.** Local exchange from the uniform electron gas of the same dimension and the same law, $\varepsilon_x(\rho) = -C_D\,\rho^{1/D}$
per electron, with C₃ = ¾(3/π)^⅓ = 0.738559 and C₄ = 16/(15√π) = 0.601802, taken from Loos and Gill's
general-D formulas for 1/r jellium (appendix B). Spins are polarized by Hund's rule (a subshell fills one spin first),
and each electron's own share is removed from both its Hartree and its exchange potential: the Hartree term by its own
orbital's cloud, the exchange term by the fully polarized exchange of that orbital alone (a Perdew–Zunger-style
correction). There is no correlation term.

### Solving one configuration

The radial equation is solved on a logarithmic grid of 700 points from r₀ = 10⁻⁵ to 150 bohr
(step h = 0.02364 in ln r) by Numerov's method on y = u/√r, with each level found by Sturm bisection on the node
count of the outward solution (90 halvings), the outward integration stopped where h²f/12 > ½ so that
Numerov cannot fake nodes in the forbidden region, and the orbital matched to an inward solution at the turning point.

For a fixed configuration (occupations of each subshell, every orbital of a subshell sharing one radial function) the
field is iterated to self-consistency: each orbital solved in the potential of the nucleus, the others' clouds and
exchange; the new clouds mixed into the old at 0.4; up to 80 iterations, stopping when the total
energy changes by less than 10⁻⁷ hartree between iterations.

**Is the stop tight enough?** A stop on the energy can leave the far density less converged than the energy is; the
plane-wave work met exactly that in its pseudopotentials' all-electron atom, where exchange carried an unconverged tail
into the potential. So 19 atoms across every row of both worlds were re-solved in their baked configurations
and then driven on from that field to a stop of 10⁻¹² hartree (appendix C, `audit-scf.mjs`). Total
energies and first ionization energies moved by at most 2.7 × 10⁻⁷ and 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ hartree, the outermost orbital
energy by 1.7 × 10⁻⁶, and Σ⟨r²⟩ (the far pull's S, and the forces between atoms) by 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ of itself; the
baked ⟨r²⟩ agree with the tight ones to 7.0 × 10⁻⁵. The density beyond about 15 bohr is not converged relatively,
but it is noise there: off by large factors only where it is 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁷ electrons per bohr, and converged to
10⁻⁶ where an atom has a loosely held s electron that puts real charge out that far. Nothing the paper quotes depends
on it; a calculation that builds a potential from the far density through exchange must converge the density
pointwise, as the pseudopotentials now do.

**Is the grid fine enough?** 11 atoms from every row of both worlds were re-solved in their baked
configurations on six other grids, changing one of the number of points (500, 1000), the inner end (10⁻⁴, 10⁻⁶ bohr) and
the outer end (100, 250 bohr) at a time (appendix C, `convergence.mjs`). First ionization energies moved by at most
1.4 × 10⁻⁴ hartree on any of them. Total energies moved by at most 6.7 × 10⁻² hartree, 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ of themselves,
the largest for our own krypton, whose 1s sits deeper than any four-dimensional atom's and is the grid's hardest case.
The paper quotes ionization energies and energy differences, not total energies.

### The ground configuration

For each Z the ground configuration is searched, not assumed. The search starts from the hydrogenic filling (subshells
in order of n, then l), solves it, and refills by the orbital energies of every subshell, occupied or not, in the field
it has just found, up to 6 rounds or until the filling stops changing. It then tries moving one or two
electrons between the open subshells, the two highest filled ones and the two lowest empty ones, solving each
candidate from the current field. A candidate counts only if its field settles: an unsettled field can report an
energy far too low, since with exchange a barely bound orbital can drift for hundreds of iterations. The lowest settled
energy is the ground state.

For 7 elements of the 4D table (88, 101–103 and 105–107) the first search landed on an unsettled
field. They were searched again seeded from both neighbours' configurations with one or two electrons added or taken,
each seed solved from scratch, and the lowest settled one kept.

The first ionization energy is ΔSCF: the ion's own ground state with an electron taken from whichever of the
3 least-bound occupied subshells leaves it lowest, relaxed from the atom's field, minus the atom's
energy. Koopmans' orbital energies are not used.

The table is 140 elements in four dimensions and 36 in ours, baked once (on GitHub's runners past
Z ≈ 80) into a single generated file, which a selftest re-solves in sample on every change.

### The terms of open subshells

The search above gives every open subshell Hund spins. Section 7 finds where that's wrong, and the table is corrected
for it. Each d- and f-block element is searched again, seeded as the repair pass seeds, and every settled candidate's
energy gets its open subshells' term correction: the lowest term less the lowest maximum-spin term. That comes from
the subshell's own repulsion on that candidate's own orbital (`atom/tools/termtable.mjs`). It is zero wherever Hund's
first rule holds. The ionization is corrected the same way on both sides. Fillings whose spin blocks are too large to
solve per candidate take the survey's verdict (section 7.2), which for them is that the rule holds.

### The counterfactual

To separate what the table owes to the law from what it owes to the geometry, every 4D element is solved a second time
with the shell theorem forced on: the clouds' potential taken as 1/max(r, s) (our kernel) while everything else, the
4D kinetic operator, the degeneracies, exchange, the search, stays as it was. Each element's search is seeded with the
real table's configuration and its neighbours' ± one electron, so the counterfactual isn't a weaker search; and the real
law is re-solved in each counterfactual configuration, to check that the real table's configuration is still the lower
one under the law. Where no candidate's field settled, a second, wider search started from every configuration in reach
(the real table's for the element and its neighbours ± one electron, the unsettled filling, and the counterfactual's own
neighbours ± one), each solved from scratch with the clouds mixed at 0.15 for up to 1500
iterations. A counterfactual atom counts as settled only if its field converged and its first ionization energy is
positive (a negative one means an electron would rather leave: the search missed a lower configuration). By that rule
112 of 140 settle, every atom up to 88; the rest (89–116) are row 6's f block and the first elements after it.

### One electron, any law

The arguments of section 2 use a separate solver for one electron in any central potential (`laws.js`): the same
radial equation and Numerov–Sturm method on a grid whose inner end can be moved, which is what tests a fall to the
centre. For V = −α/r² it finds no level below α = ½ on any grid and, above it, a lowest level that scales as 1/r₀²
(section 2.1); for V = −1/rᵖ it gives the splittings within each shell (section 3.1). Its check is 4D hydrogen:
−0.22222222 against −2/9.

### Checks

Every method above has a known-answer test in the selftest, run on every change: hydrogen in both worlds (block 1), the
radial solver (2), the kernel against direct integration (3), exchange against the electron-gas constants (4, 18), the
ground search (5, 7), two-electron atoms against an independent Gaussian Hartree–Fock code in four dimensions and MP2
against PySCF in ours (17, 43), our table against measured values (6: 32 of 36 configurations; ionization to a
4.3 % median error), and this paper's own claims recomputed from the bake (67).

## 6 · Checks against what is known

**6.1 Hydrogen.** One electron needs no search and no exchange, and four-dimensional hydrogen has an exact answer:
$-Z^2/2(n + \tfrac12)^2$ hartree, so $-2/9$ for the ground state. The solver gives −0.22222.

**6.2 Two electrons.** Helium-like atoms in four dimensions are checked against an independent code, Hartree–Fock in a
Gaussian basis written for any dimension (`gauss.js`), and the same atoms in ours against PySCF at the MP2 level
(selftest blocks 17 and 43). The two codes share no part of the radial solver.

**6.3 Our own table.** The same solver, the same law (in ours 1/r is Gauss's) and the same search, run in three
dimensions, gives 32 of 36 of our measured ground configurations. The four it misses, titanium, vanadium, cobalt and nickel, each take one
d electron too many against 4s, the known lean of local exchange toward d. The misses have one cause. Moving an electron from 4s into 3d comes out
too cheap in every 3d atom we can compare (eV, the solver against measured: Sc 0.14 against 1.43, Ti −0.89 against 0.81, Fe 0.51 against 0.86, Co −0.35 against 0.43, Ni −1.16 against 0.03), short by 0.35–1.70
eV and a mean 1.06, always in d's favour. That is local exchange without correlation. Resolving every open
subshell's whole term structure doesn't remove it. With that correction (the lowest term less the average of the
maximum-spin arrangements, which is what a spherically averaged field stands for), the bias stays at 1.07 eV and
the configurations get worse, 26 of 32 against 28 of 32. So the paper corrects only Hund's first rule
(section 7), the one thing a spin-polarized averaged field cannot represent. Its first ionization energies are off by a
median 4.3 % and at most 16.2 % (figure A2). That is the accuracy to expect of the 4D table: a method
that gets our transition metals mostly right and our ionizations to a few percent, not a spectroscopic one.

**6.4 Ions.** Each ion of ours searched for its own ground state, rather than made by taking one electron from the
atom's configuration, changes no first ionization. The same search for anions gives our electron affinities where
the extra electron is bound by the field and exchange: the p-block acceptors (C 1.32 against 1.262, Si 1.30 against 1.39, Ge 1.25 against 1.233, Al 0.40 against 0.433, F 2.80 against 3.401, Cl 3.15 against 3.613, O 0.71 against 1.461 eV, measured second). It
also finds every anion that should be unbound to be unbound: the noble gases, beryllium, magnesium and nitrogen. It
fails where correlation does the binding (H -0.33 against 0.754, Li -0.08 against 0.618, Na -0.02 against 0.548, P -0.10 against 0.746). In four dimensions, then, an affinity above about 0.7 eV is to
be believed and a smaller one is not (Rienstra-Kiracofe et al. 2002 for the measured values).

**6.5 Numbers.** Tightening the solver's stop or changing its grid moves no ionization energy by a millihartree
(section 5 and appendix C).

## 7 · Hund's first rule in four dimensions

The solver gives each open subshell the most parallel spins it can hold. That is Hund's first rule, and in ours it is
the known answer for the ground terms of free atoms. In four dimensions it is an assumption, and for some fillings it
is wrong.

**7.1 How the terms are found.** For each open subshell of each ground configuration, its orbitals are the degree-$l$
harmonics on the 3-sphere, $(l + 1)^2$ of them (4 for p, 9 for d, 16 for f). The repulsion between two of its
electrons is the law's $1/|x - y|$, projected exactly onto the harmonics of degree $0$ to $2l$, with the radial parts
integrated over the atom's own orbital. Every arrangement of the subshell's electrons with a given $M_S$ is set up and
the lowest energy found (Lanczos, matrix-free; a 4D d⁹ block has 15 876 arrangements). A term of spin $S$ appears in
every block with $M_S \le S$, so the ground term's spin is the largest $M_S$ whose block still reaches the lowest
energy. In ours this reproduces Racah's term separations for d² and d³ to the wavenumber, and the known ground terms of
Cr³⁺, Mn²⁺, Pr³⁺ and Gd³⁺. Over all 23 open subshells of our table, maximum spin is lowest, as it should be.

**7.2 Where it fails.** In four dimensions all 36 open p subshells of the table keep the rule, and so do the d
fillings d¹, d³–d¹², d¹⁴, d¹⁵, d¹⁷. The two exceptions are d² and its mirror d¹⁶, in all three d rows: element 26 (3d², 0.40 eV), element 39 (3d¹⁶, 0.77 eV), element 54 (4d², 0.30 eV), element 66 (4d¹⁶, 0.58 eV), element 114 (5d², 0.36 eV), element 126 (5d¹⁶, 0.63 eV). In each the ground
term is a spin singlet of ten states, and the triplet the solver assumed lies 0.30–0.77 eV above it. In the f block
4f³ (element 83) fails too, and so does its mirror 4f²⁹ (element 108), three short of a full shell. Both have a
ground term of spin ½, 0.15 and 0.26 eV below the quartet. Every other f filling keeps the rule. For
f², f⁴, f⁵, f²⁸, f³⁰, f³¹ every spin was checked; for f⁶–f²⁵ only the highest two or three, because the lower-spin
blocks run to 10⁶–10⁸ arrangements. There the result is a bound: no lower term among the spins that could be run.
Two fillings (elements 102 and 106) didn't finish in the runner's time.

**7.3 Why it fails.** It isn't the law. On element 26's own orbital Gauss's $1/r^2$ gives the same order, with the
singlet 0.82 eV below the triplet, against 0.40 eV under $1/r$; the pinned law makes the failure smaller,
not larger. The cause is the shell itself. Four-dimensional d orbitals form the representation (1,1) of SO(4) ≅
SU(2) × SU(2)/ℤ₂. Two electrons in them make spatially symmetric states (2,2) ⊕ (2,0) ⊕ (0,2) ⊕ (1,1) ⊕ (0,0), all spin
singlets (25, 10, 9 and 1 states), and antisymmetric ones (2,1) ⊕ (1,2) ⊕ (1,0) ⊕ (0,1), triplets (30 and 6). The
singlet that comes lowest is the ten-state (2,0) ⊕ (0,2). For two electrons in a d subshell each term's energy is
exactly $F^0 + a_2F^2 + a_4F^4$. The $F^n$ are the radial parts of the repulsion and depend on the orbital. The
$a_n = \langle C_n(\cos\gamma)\rangle$ over the term ($\gamma$ is the angle between the two electrons seen from the
nucleus) depend only on the term. $a_2$ measures how much the term lets the electrons line up along a common axis. The
ten-state singlet holds them nearest right angles, $\langle\cos^2\gamma\rangle$ = 0.125, half of random
(0.250), where the best triplet reaches 0.188. It lies below every triplet whenever $F^4/F^2 <$ 5/3.
Element 26's orbital has $F^4/F^2$ = 0.39 under the law and 0.65 under Gauss's, so the rule breaks
either way. In ours the triplet ³F is the term that keeps the electrons nearest right angles (0.225, against
¹D's 0.292 and random's 0.333), and it is the lowest for every value of $F^4/F^2$. Titanium's d² has ³F lowest
and its first singlet 1.25 eV up. Pauli keeps same-spin electrons apart, which is the usual reason for Hund's
rule; four-dimensional space gives paired spins a way to stay apart that is better still. In SO(4) terms, every
rotation splits into a left and a right half, and a d orbital carries one unit of each. The singlet adds the two
electrons' left halves and cancels their right ones, or the other way round. Three-dimensional rotations don't split,
so ours has no such state. An interactive version is at four.mino.mobi/atom/hund.html.

**7.4 What it does to the table.** Where the rule fails, the solver's energy for that configuration is the
maximum-spin state's, too high by the gap. The table in section 8 corrects that. Every d- and f-block element
(92 of them) was searched again, with the neighbours' configurations as extra seeds (49–65 settled
candidates each). Every candidate got its open subshells' gaps added, and the candidates were ranked again, with and
without the correction, so that a change from the wider search is told apart from one from the terms. **The terms
change no ground configuration.** They lower the eight Hund-breaking atoms' energies, and they move first ionizations
in pairs. An atom whose own ground term gains the gap holds its electron harder: 54 (6.41 → 6.71), 66 (18.82 → 19.40), 114 (6.92 → 7.27), 126 (24.92 → 25.55) eV. The next element,
whose ion lands on the broken filling, gives one up more easily: 55 (8.28 → 7.91), 67 (20.56 → 19.93), 115 (9.28 → 8.83), 127 (27.23 → 26.56) eV. That is 0.30–0.67 eV either way.
The wider search found one configuration the bake had missed. Element 82 is 4f¹ 5d¹ 6s², 0.36 eV below the
bake's 4f² 6s², which is our cerium's kind; its ionization goes 7.03 → 7.39 eV. The table that follows is the
corrected one (`data/table4.csv`). The Hund-spin table it replaces is supplement S1 (`data/table4-hundspin.csv`).
How far to trust each configuration follows from section 6.3. Take a bias of about a volt toward d and f: a ground
configuration with a competitor holding fewer d and f electrons within a volt of it could be the other way round.
11 of the 92 d- and f-block elements have one: 30 (3d⁶ 4s², 0.55 eV up), 37 (3d¹³ 4s², 0.55 eV up), 53 (5s² 5p¹, 0.01 eV up), 58 (4d⁶ 5s², 0.20 eV up), 61 (4d⁹ 5s², 0.25 eV up), 64 (4d¹³ 5s¹, 0.95 eV up), 107 (5p⁸ 6s², 0.20 eV up), 108 (5p⁸ 6s², 0.79 eV up), 109 (5p⁸ 6s², 0.57 eV up), 122 (5d¹⁰ 6s², 0.54 eV up), 124 (5d¹³ 6s¹, 0.55 eV up).

## 8 · The table

**8.1 Rows and noble gases.** The table's rows hold 2, 10, 10, 28, 28, 60 elements (and 2 of the next by
element 140), and its noble gases are elements 2, 12, 22, 50, 78, 138, each a peak of the first ionization energy (figures
1 and 4). Those are the rows the generalized Madelung rule of Négadi and Kibler (1996) predicts for four dimensions.
To our knowledge this is the first self-consistent table that confirms them. Part III asks how much of that the law
decides.

**8.2 The hardest-held electron isn't a noble gas's.** Element 128 has an 18-electron d shell, full, with nothing
outside it. It holds its outermost electron at 29.56 eV, harder than its row's noble gas 138 (26.71 eV) and
harder than any other atom in the table. Element 68, the same kind a row up, comes within a volt of its noble gas 78
(22.32 eV against 23.10). Ours goes the other way: palladium's full 4d¹⁰ gives up an electron at 8.3 eV,
xenon at 12.1. Searching each ion for its own ground state leaves element 128's ionization where
it was. Seven other ions do rearrange, and their ionizations drop: 36 (11.42 → 10.94), 93 (9.14 → 8.90), 94 (9.20 → 8.43), 95 (9.27 → 7.99), 103 (9.96 → 9.67), 104 (10.05 → 9.29), 105 (10.13 → 8.92) eV. The main table carries those. Section 9 shows the law does it.

**8.3 Inside the rows.** Figure 5 draws six atoms in profile: their radial densities, and what each one's outermost
orbital looks like on the 3-sphere (figure 3). Where the filling departs from the simple order, and how the
ionization energy and the radius run with Z, are in the data files (table4.csv).

# Part III · What the law does


## 9 · The table again, with the shell theorem forced on

Part I chose the law; Part II solved the table under it. To see which of the table's features the law decides, every
4D element was solved a second time with one thing changed: the clouds' potential taken as if the shell theorem held
(our kernel, $1/\max(r, s)$), and everything else, the four-dimensional kinetic energy, the degeneracies, exchange,
the search, left as it was (section 5). Of the 140 elements, 112 settle, every one up to element
88. The rest, elements 89–116, row 6's f block and the first elements after it, have no settled
ground state under the shell theorem from any starting configuration tried. They are left out, so this part's
statements about the rows hold through row 5.

**9.1 The rows are the geometry's.** With the shell theorem forced on, the first 24 elements keep every configuration,
and the noble gases close the same rows at elements 2, 12, 22, 50, 78, 138 (figure 6). The lengths of the rows, 2, 10, 10,
28, 28, come from four-dimensional space's degeneracies, $2(l + 1)^2$ to a subshell. They don't come from the law
between charges, so long as that law keeps a shell together (section 3.1).

**9.2 What fills inside the rows is the law's.** Of the settled atoms, 57 change configuration, and the
first is element 25, the first d element. Under the shell theorem p beats d. Element 25 takes 4s² 4p¹
where the law gives 3d¹ 4s², and the change runs on through the d and f blocks. In every changed atom the law's own
configuration is still the lower one when solved under the law, so the difference is the law's, not a weaker search.

## 10 · Partial screening

In ours an outer electron sees the nucleus screened by every inner electron whole: the shell theorem makes an inner
cloud act as its charge at the centre. In four dimensions an inner cloud screens only partly, because its pull at
radius $r$ is $k(t)/r$ of a point charge's with $k < 1$ (section 4.2). The outer electrons see more of the nucleus.

**10.1 How much harder.** Across the 110 atoms past helium that settle under both, the law holds the
outermost electron a median 2.54 times as hard as the shell theorem would, from 1.06 to
9.55 times. Among the noble gases the ratio grows from 1.09 (helium) to 2.90 (element
138).

**10.2 Element 128.** The largest ratio is element 128's. Its 5d¹⁸ shell, full with nothing outside it, holds its
electron at 29.56 eV under the law and at 3.1 eV under the shell theorem. With the shell theorem the
noble gases are again the hardest-held atoms, as ours are. The table's hardest-held electron (section 8.2) is partial
screening at its strongest: a full shell whose own cloud hides the nucleus from it least.

**10.3 Negative ions.** Partial screening holds an extra electron harder too. One electron short of a full p shell
(p⁷ in four dimensions), atoms bind an extra electron by 3.4, 5.7, 7.8, 10.3, 12.9 eV going down the group, rising with every row,
where ours stay level (F 3.401, Cl 3.613, Br 3.364 eV, measured). The largest affinity in the table is 12.9 eV (element 137), and
80 of the 140 atoms bind an extra electron by more than the 0.7 eV section 6.4 trusts. The light noble gases
(2, 12, 22) don't hold one at all: their anions lie 7, 14, 12 eV above the atom. The heavier ones come out barely
bound (50: 0.05, 78: 0.23, 138: 0.45 eV), too little to call. In ours this method underbinds anions like these, whose extra electron is s.

## 11 · Neutral atoms aren't silent

Under the shell theorem a neutral atom is invisible from outside its cloud. Here it isn't. A spherical cloud of
charge felt from outside gives $-q\,k(t)/s$ with $k = 1 - t^2/8 - \dots$ (appendix A). The nucleus and the electrons
cancel in the first term, and what remains, for an electron at distance $s$, is a pull $-\sum\langle r^2\rangle/8s^3$
over the atom's electrons. The solved noble gases follow it: at 30 bohr the full cloud's potential and the far form
agree to 0.22 %. Between two atoms the same failure gives a permanent attraction
$-3S_AS_B/64R^5$ ($S = \sum\langle r^2\rangle$), with no dipole needed, which outranges London's $R^{-6}$. The papers
that follow take it up: noble gases that condense far above where ours do, and molecules held differently.

## 12 · Limitations

**The law's own.** The force acts instantly (section 4.3), so only statics are safe; this paper has nothing that
moves. Heavy atoms would need relativity, which the law has given up for the force between charges; the table past
about element 100 is first-pass for that reason, and the innermost Dirac level of a bare nucleus would dive near
Z ≈ 230 for a nucleus of 4–5 fm, as a potential problem, not one met here. Nuclei are declared stable to Z = 140.

**The method's.** Local exchange and no correlation, which in ours favours d by about a volt (section 6.3); in four
dimensions that leaves the configurations section 7.4 lists in doubt. Every subshell's cloud is
averaged over the sphere. The terms of open subshells are resolved only to first order, on the solver's orbitals, and
only where the rule fails (section 7). The counterfactual table leaves row 6's f block unsettled (section 9).

**What isn't claimed.** That four-dimensional chemistry looks like ours: the next papers take up bonds, liquids and
crystals under the same law.

## 13 · Conclusion

A world with four large dimensions of space has to choose its law between charges, because Gauss's law gives it no
atoms. Pinned at $1/r$, the only power law that keeps a shell together, it has atoms, and they have a periodic table:
rows of 2, 10, 10, 28, 28, 60, noble gases at 2, 12, 22, 50, 78 and 138, as the generalized Madelung rule predicts.
The rows are the geometry's. Everything that fills inside them from the first d element on is the law's, because in
four dimensions $1/r$ isn't harmonic and an inner cloud screens only partly: outer electrons are held about two and a
half times harder, the table's hardest-held electron belongs to a full d shell rather than a noble gas, and a neutral
atom pulls from afar. And four-dimensional space breaks Hund's first rule for the d² and d¹⁶ fillings and for 4f³ and 4f²⁹,
whatever the law.

# Appendices


## A · The 4D kernel

A thin spherical shell of unit charge and radius $s$, felt at radius $r$, gives the potential $k(t)/\max(r, s)$,
where $t = \min(r, s)/\max(r, s)$ and $k$ is the law's $1/|x - y|$ averaged over the shell. On the 3-sphere the
average over directions carries the weight $\tfrac{2}{\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$, so

$$k(t) = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi \frac{\sin^2\theta\,d\theta}{\sqrt{1 + t^2 - 2t\cos\theta}}.$$

In ours the same average, with weight $\tfrac12\sin\theta\,d\theta$, is exactly 1 for every $t$: the shell theorem. In
four dimensions it isn't. The integral has a closed form in the complete elliptic integrals $K$ and $E$ of modulus $t$,

$$k(t) = \frac{4\,[(1 + t^2)\,E(t) - (1 - t^2)\,K(t)]}{3\pi t^2},$$

which gives $k(1) = 8/3\pi$ (since $E(1) = 1$), and the series

$$k(t) = 1 - \frac{t^2}{8} - \frac{t^4}{64} - \frac{5t^6}{1024} - \frac{35t^8}{16384} - \dots$$

Each term is $t^n$ times the average of the Legendre polynomial $P_n(\cos\theta)$ over the 3-sphere; the odd ones
vanish. The solver evaluates $k$ by Simpson's rule in $\theta$ with 400 intervals, tabulated at
2001 points of $t$ and interpolated. The closed form agrees with that quadrature to 2.7 × 10⁻¹⁵
for $t$ up to 0.9 (ledger `kernelclosed`); nearer 1 the quadrature's own error dominates, a few parts in $10^7$.

The series' first correction is the far pull of section 11. A cloud of $N$ electrons around a nucleus $+Z$, seen from
a distance $s$ outside it, gives $\big(Z - N + \sum_i \langle r_i^2\rangle / 8s^2 + \dots\big)/s$. A neutral atom
therefore acts on an electron through $-\sum\langle r^2\rangle/8s^3$, and two neutral atoms through
$-3S_AS_B/64R^5$ (section 11). Figure A1 draws $k$, and the potential inside and outside a shell.

## B · The 4D electron gas

The solver's exchange is the local form of the uniform electron gas of the same dimension and the same law. In $D$
dimensions a spin-unpolarized Fermi sea of density $\rho$ has $\rho = 2\,\Omega_D k_F^D/(2\pi)^D$, with $\Omega_D$ the
volume of the unit ball ($\pi^2/2$ for $D = 4$). Its kinetic energy per volume is $\tfrac{D}{D + 2}\,\rho\,k_F^2/2$:
$\tfrac{3}{10}(3\pi^2)^{2/3}\rho^{5/3}$ in ours (Thomas–Fermi's 2.8712), $\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\rho^{3/2}$ in four dimensions.
Its exchange energy per volume is $-C_D\,\rho^{1 + 1/D}$. In ours $C_3 = \tfrac34(3/\pi)^{1/3}$ = 0.738559,
Dirac's constant. In four dimensions under the pinned $1/r$, with the Fermi sea's density matrix built on the Bessel
function $J_2$ and the integral $\int_0^\infty J_2(x)^2\,x^{-2}\,dx = 4/15\pi$, it is $C_4 = 16/15\sqrt\pi$ =
0.601802. These agree with Loos and Gill's (2016) expressions for the $D$-dimensional gas. The selftest checks
the textbook values in ours and the 4D integral (blocks 4 and 18). The potential each electron feels is
$v_x = -(1 + 1/D)\,C_D\,\rho^{1/D}$, spin-polarized as in section 5 (each spin's own density doubled), with each
electron's own share taken out.

## C · Numerical convergence

**The solver's stop.** The self-consistent field stops when the total energy changes by less than 10⁻⁷
hartree between iterations. Re-solving 19 atoms (4D 2, 4D 7, 4D 12, 4D 13, 4D 22, 4D 26, 4D 50, 4D 51, 4D 68, 4D 78, 4D 101, 4D 128, 4D 138, ours 2, ours 10, ours 11, ours 18, ours 26, ours 36) with the stop at 10⁻¹²
moves no total energy by more than 2.7 × 10⁻⁷ hartree and no first ionization by more than 2.8 × 10⁻⁷
(ledger `converged`).

**The radial grid.** The baked grid has 700 points from 10⁻⁵ to 150 bohr, logarithmic with
step 0.02364. 11 atoms (4D 2, 4D 12, 4D 13, 4D 22, 4D 50, 4D 78, 4D 128, 4D 138, ours 10, ours 18, ours 36) were re-solved on six other grids, each changing one parameter
(ledger `grid`):

| change from the baked grid | largest \|ΔE\| (hartree) | largest \|Δ ionization\| (hartree) |
|---|---|---|
| N 500 | 2.0 × 10⁻² | 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ |
| N 1000 | 1.0 × 10⁻² | 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ |
| r₀ 10⁻⁴ | 6.7 × 10⁻² | 3.8 × 10⁻⁵ |
| r₀ 10⁻⁶ | 5.4 × 10⁻³ | 4.2 × 10⁻⁵ |
| r_max 100 | 1.0 × 10⁻³ | 6.9 × 10⁻⁶ |
| r_max 250 | 1.3 × 10⁻³ | 8.9 × 10⁻⁶ |

The total energies of the heaviest atoms move by up to 6.7 × 10⁻² hartree, 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ of themselves, with the
innermost point. The ionization energies, the differences the paper's chemistry uses, move by at most 1.4 × 10⁻⁴
hartree.

## D · The law calculations

Section 2's arguments use a separate one-electron solver (`laws.js`), so that the grid's inner end can be moved. It
uses the radial equation with $L = l + (D - 3)/2$ on a logarithmic grid of 6000 points, counts the nodes of
an outward Numerov solution at a trial energy, and bisects on the count to $10^{-13}$ relative; a level that falls with
the inner end of the grid is a fall to the centre. Its check is 4D hydrogen, −0.22222222 hartree against $-2/9$.

**Gauss's $-\alpha/r^2$.** At $\alpha$ = 0.45 there is no bound level on any grid. At $\alpha$ = 0.7 the lowest level is
−5.87 × 10³, −5.87 × 10⁵ and −5.87 × 10⁷ hartree with the inner end at $10^{-3}$, $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-5}$ bohr:
$\varepsilon r_0^2$ = −0.00587 and −0.00587, a fall to the centre set by $r_0$ (ledger `gauss`). The boundary
between the two is Hardy's constant $((D - 2)/2)^2 = 1$ (Barbatis 2023), which with the kinetic energy $\tfrac12|\nabla\psi|^2$
puts the critical $\alpha$ at $\tfrac12$ (Landau and Lifshitz 1977, §35).

**Power laws $-1/r^p$.** The splitting of 2p from 2s, as a fraction of the shell's binding, is −6.2 % at
$p = 0.8$, 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ % at $p = 1$ and +15.4 % at $p = 1.2$. For 3d against 3s it is −9.2 % and
+21.9 % (ledger `uniqueness`). Only $p = 1$ keeps a shell together.

## E · Reproducing every number

Every number in the text is read by `papers/p1/build.mjs` from one of the files below, and the selftest (block 67)
fails if any claim in `ledger.json` stops holding or any generated file is stale. What made each file:

| file | made by | where |
|---|---|---|
| `atom/js/table.js` (the bake; supplement S1) | `atom/tools/bake.mjs`, then `--repair` for 88, 101–103, 105–107 | GitHub's runners, six minutes a shard |
| `data/termtable.json` (the main table) | `atom/tools/termtable.mjs`, collected by `termtable-collect.mjs` | runner run `hund-f-and-terms` |
| `data/hund.json` | `atom/tools/hund.mjs survey`, collected by `hund-collect.mjs` | sandbox (p, d, first f) and runner run `hund-f` |
| `data/hund-law.json` | `papers/p1/hundlaw.mjs` | a minute |
| `data/promotion3.json` | `termtable.mjs` with `TERM_MODE=full` on ours, `promotion-collect.mjs` | sandbox, minutes |
| `data/shelltable.json` | `atom/tools/lawtable.mjs shell`, `repair`, `bake` | runner runs `lawtable-shell`, `lawtable-repair` |
| `data/audit-scf.json`, `data/convergence.json` | `audit-scf.mjs`, `convergence.mjs` | runner |
| `data/profiles.json` | `profiles.mjs` | sandbox |
| `data/table3.*`, `data/table4.*`, `figdata/`, `figures/`, `ledger.json`, `draft/` | `build.mjs` | seconds |
| `draft/*.html`, `draft/paper.pdf` | `page.mjs` (pandoc), `pdf.cjs` | seconds |

`papers/p1/reproduce.mjs` re-solves a sample of atoms from the solver and checks them against the paper's data;
`--all` re-solves every element. The runner's logs, with each command's exit status, are kept on the repository's
`atom4-data` branch under `runs/`. The code is mirrored at a tagged version for citation.
